profiled_workloads.selection_reason: Lowest eval speedup (1.244x) and smallest shape; representative of the small-input, host/launch-bound regime that dispatches to the owner kernel.
Highest eval latency (2.546 ms) and representative of the wide-row sorted-segment regime, where the bulk of the remaining absolute time sits.
Mid-size boundary of the sorted-segment regime (1024 columns, still sort path); used to check whether the wide-row split scales with row width and whether device time accounts for the full call.

findings.label: Wide-row time is dominated by the sorted-key pass, which runs mostly on the Scalar pipe
findings.backend_detail: msprof op_summary perf counters, AI_VECTOR_CORE task, 100 measured invocations (2048 blocks per invocation)
findings.inference: At 2048 columns the key pass consumes 1918.0 us of the 2544.1 us mean device time (75%) and spends 1711.5 us on the Scalar pipe against 205.5 us on Vector and 24.5 us on MTE2; it is neither memory-bound nor vector-bound. The kernel (main.py lines 176-199) is one fused sequence per row: int64 index load and fp32 key build, `_al.sort` over a B=2048 fp32 row, an on-chip gather of the values, a full-width fp32 `tl.cumsum`, then two B-wide stores. The metric cannot say which of those ingredients is scalarized, only that the scalar pipe owns the critical path.

findings.label: The round-3 on-chip rewrite left the combine pass vector-bound and secondary
findings.inference: The 12-step branchless search plus run-boundary lookup (15 on-chip gathers per row, main.py lines 219-242) now runs as vector work: 546.6 us of vector time out of 627.4 us AIV time, with only 64.1 us scalar and 25.1 us MTE2. This is direct support for the frozen round-3 hypothesis: moving the search off data-dependent global loads removed the dominant cost of that pass, so further wide-row effort should not be spent on the search itself.

findings.label: Key-pass scalar cost scales with total elements, and the whole call is device-bound at 1024 columns
findings.inference: At 1024 columns the same split appears: key pass 493.1 us at 88.9% scalar, combine pass 191.3 us at 80.7% vector, total 684.4 us against an eval latency of 685.7 us, so at this size the measured call is essentially the two device tasks. Scalar time in the key pass grows from 437.3 us (1024 rows x B=1024) to 1711.5 us (2048 rows x B=2048), i.e. 3.92x for 4x the elements, which is consistent with a roughly constant scalar cost per element rather than a fixed per-row overhead. The exact growth law (O(B) versus O(B log B)) cannot be separated from two points.

findings.label: Small-input workloads are bounded by host-side call cost, not by the device kernel
findings.inference: The bf16 128x128 call dispatches a single `_scatter_add_owner_kernel` (128 blocks, one per row) that takes 13.9 us of device time, i.e. about 14% of the 99.7 us eval latency; the remaining ~86% is outside the captured device task. Because only one device task exists and it is short, the small-case speedups (1.24x-1.37x) are capped by per-call host cost (parameter marshalling, the tuple-grid launch, and the fresh output allocation required by the out-of-place contract), not by kernel math. Within the kernel the vector (0.60) and scalar (0.50) pipes are both active on a 14 us task, so this is not a device bottleneck worth optimizing first.

performance_interpretation: Round 3 validates its hypothesis: the wide-row workloads that regressed in round 2 recovered from 19.48 ms to 2.54 ms (2048 columns) and from 2.85 ms to 0.686 ms (1024 columns), inside the predicted 1.25x/1.32x band, lifting geo_mean from 0.4111 to 1.2957. Profiling shows the win came exactly where predicted: the combine pass is now vector-bound (87% vector, 626 us) and the remaining wide-row cost is the separate key/sort pass (1918 us, 89% scalar at 2048 columns; 493 us, 89% scalar at 1024 columns). Since the call is device-bound at those sizes, halving the key pass would move the six wide timing workloads substantially, whereas the three 128-column workloads are launch-bound and would need host-side work. No Roofline or peak-utilization claim is made: the pipeline ratios are marginal activity statistics and are not additive.

next_experiment.action_description: Attribute, then remove, the scalar phase of `_scatter_add_sort_key_kernel` (candidate main.py lines 176-199). First run a bounded, numerically checked target-side probe at the exact wide configuration (rows=2048, B=2048, fp32 key row) that times the three isolatable ingredients of that fused kernel separately: `_al.sort` on the `target*B+lane` fp32 row, the on-chip `tl.gather(values, src_lane)`, and the full-width fp32 `tl.cumsum` of the reordered values. The docstring's ingredient table covers sort (0.20 ms at 2048x2048), gather (0.04 ms), histogram and integer div/mod, but never measures the fp32 cumsum, while the fused kernel spends 1711.5 us on the scalar pipe -- so the cumsum is the leading suspect and the sort is the alternative. Apply exactly one replacement based on that attribution: if the cumsum dominates, replace the full-width prefix with a blocked two-level prefix (in-block scan of width 64 plus a serial carry over the 32 block sums, consuming only run-boundary prefix differences); if the sort dominates, drop the full sort and derive the run boundaries with the already-measured owner-style grouping. Keep the fp32 key encoding, the ascending-lane accumulation order and the single rounding on store, and keep the existing dispatch (owner <=256, sort <=4096, atomic otherwise).
next_experiment.expected_impact: Diagnostic first: it decides between two very different fixes instead of sweeping. Then, on the six wide timing workloads, the scalar time of the key pass (1711.5 us at 2048 columns, 437.3 us at 1024 columns) is what sits in front of an already vector-bound combine pass (626 us / 191 us), so removing most of it is the largest remaining device-side lever; the 2.54 ms and 0.686 ms workloads are device-bound, so device savings transfer to eval latency. No speedup is claimed until a full KGS evaluation measures it, and the 128-column workloads are not expected to change because they never enter this path.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: A blocked prefix changes the summation association of the prefix array; only differences at run boundaries are consumed, so cancellation error could break the fp32 tolerance (1e-4) on the wide shapes even though the small correctness shapes still pass -- validate the wide shapes numerically, not only the 9 correctness workloads. Dropping the sort risks changing the accumulation order the fp32 reference reproduces. A probe kernel must be numerically checked before its timing is used, and ingredient timings from isolated probes are not eval latency. Rollback: keep the round-3 source (sha256 c006dfde0718d6f017c79fea38b9735ddbdc3047810a4a92da87b7ba4dd6b5a0, geo_mean 1.2957) as the accepted best and revert any edit that fails correctness or does not reduce the measured key-pass scalar time.
success_criteria: The attribution probe at rows=2048/B=2048 is numerically checked and reports per-ingredient device time, and a single ingredient accounts for the majority of the key pass's scalar time -- or all three are shown cheap, which falsifies the scalar-phase hypothesis and stops this line of work.
After the edit, msprof shows the wide-row key pass aiv_scalar_time_us well below the recorded 1711.5 us (timing-5) / 437.3 us (timing-1) while the combine pass stays vector-bound.

All 9 KGS correctness workloads PASS, and the six wide timing shapes are additionally re-verified numerically against the PyTorch reference with the frozen tolerances, run twice and once with a changed stream.
Headline geo_mean is >= 1.2957 (round-3 value) with no wide timing workload latency regression.

warnings: The instruction-level request for scatter_add-timing-5 was cancelled by the service during profiling (RUN_CANCELLED, reason_code server_operation_cancelled), so the scalar phase inside `_scatter_add_sort_key_kernel` is not attributed to a source line; all statements about which ingredient is scalarized are inference, not measurement.
msprof pipeline ratios are marginal activity statistics; they are not peak utilization, are not additive across pipes, and are not used here as a time decomposition.
Eval speedups and latencies are taken from the frozen evaluation snapshot; profiler timings (13.9 us / 684 us / 2544 us) are diagnostic only and never replace eval latency.
open_questions: Which ingredient of `_scatter_add_sort_key_kernel` -- `_al.sort` on fp32 keys, `tl.gather`, or the full-width fp32 `tl.cumsum` -- produces the 1712 us of scalar time at 2048 columns?

For the 128-column workload, how much of the 99.7 us call is host launch/marshalling versus the mandatory fresh output allocation? Metrics capture only the 13.9 us device task, so this needs a host-side probe.
Does the key pass cost grow as O(B) or O(B log B)? Two widths are not enough to separate the two growth laws.
